displayQuote: It does not matter how slowly you go, as long as you do not stop

meta.title: Who really said "It does not matter how slowly you go"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not in the Analects, and not Confucius. It is a modern English saying with no located author. The passage it is said to paraphrase — Analects Book 9 on the mound one basket short — says something much harder: the stopping is your own doing.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It does not matter how slowly you go'?
meta.ogDescription: No Analects passage says this. The real Confucius line about the unfinished mound is about responsibility, not patience — and the difference is the whole point.

answer.label: Not Confucius — a modern saying with no located author
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · modern English, no located first appearance
answer.sourceLine: This sentence appears nowhere in the Analects or in any other text associated with Confucius, and no earlier author has ever been produced for it. What it is usually said to paraphrase is a real passage — Analects, Book 9 (‘Zi Han’), the passage beginning 譬如為山, numbered 19 in the Chinese Text Project and cited in many editions as 9.18. But that passage is not encouragement about pace. It is about who is to blame.

source.heading: The passage it is supposed to be

docMeta.dd: 5th–3rd century BCE, by disciples and their successors

source.excerpt: 譬如為山，未成一簣，止，吾止也；譬如平地，雖覆一簣，進，吾往也。
trail: We looked for the popular sentence in the Analects itself. It is not there — not in Book 9, not anywhere — and it is not in the Doctrine of the Mean, the Great Learning or Mencius either. Nobody who circulates it cites a book and chapter, which is the usual signature of a saying that has none the Chinese text ↗.

The passage everyone points to is the mound. Legge’s 1861 English: ‘The prosecution of learning may be compared to what may happen in raising a mound. If there want but one basket of earth to complete the work, and I stop, the stopping is my own work. It may be compared to throwing down the earth on the level ground. Though but one basketful is thrown at a time, the advancing with it is my own going forward.’

Read those two halves against each other and the sentiment is nothing like the fortune cookie. Confucius is not saying slow progress still counts. He is saying that both outcomes are yours — quitting one basket from the summit is your doing, and so is inching forward on flat ground. The modern line offers comfort; the real one hands you the responsibility.
source.excerptNote: Confucius’s Chinese. The two clauses are deliberately symmetrical: 止，吾止也 (I stop, the stopping is mine) against 進，吾往也 (I advance, the going is mine). Whatever happens, it is you who did it.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Confucius
author.bio: Confucius (Kǒng Fūzǐ, 551–479 BCE) wrote nothing himself. Everything we have of him is the Analects, a compilation of remembered sayings assembled by disciples and their students after his death — short, abrupt, often obscure, and frequently more demanding than comforting. That gap between the real texture of the text and the world’s idea of ‘ancient Eastern wisdom’ is exactly where fake Confucius quotes live. If a line is smooth, encouraging and reads like it was written for a poster, it is almost certainly not his.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Three separate things get collapsed into one here: a modern English saying, a real Confucian passage, and a genuine Chinese proverb that is not Confucius’s either.

items.why: It is absent from the Analects and from every other text in the Confucian canon, and no Chinese original has ever been produced. Nor has anyone found an earlier English author. It circulates entirely on the strength of the name attached to it search the text ↗.

Confucius’s image is a mound left one basket of earth short of finished. His conclusion is not that slow progress is fine; it is ‘the stopping is my own work.’ He then completes the symmetry with the opposite case: one basketful onto flat ground, and ‘the advancing with it is my own going forward.’ It is a statement about agency, not about patience.

items.scope: The Chinese proverb people reach for
items.why: The saying 不怕慢，只怕站 — ‘do not fear going slowly, fear standing still’ — is much closer to the English line in sense, and it is a genuine Chinese proverb. It is anonymous folk wisdom, though, with no line back to Confucius.

The Analects almost never reassures. It sets standards, notes failures and leaves you to it. A sentence whose whole function is to make the reader feel better about slow progress is stylistically foreign to the book before you even check the index.

misattribution.truthLine: Not Confucius, and not in the Analects. The passage it is supposed to paraphrase — Book 9, the mound left one basket short — says the stopping is your own doing, which is a much harder thought read it ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is perfectly built for the moment you are behind and know it. The saying removes speed as a measure of worth and replaces it with a single binary you can still pass: are you moving at all? That is genuinely useful, which is why it has outlived every attempt to correct it.

The irony is that the passage it borrows its authority from does the opposite. Confucius takes the same image of incremental effort and uses it to close off the excuse: if you stopped, you stopped, and that was you. The paraphrase kept the mound and threw away the point.
context.detailsSummary: The two halves of Analects, Book 9
detailsBody: First half: you are raising a mound and stop one basket of earth short. Legge — ‘the stopping is my own work.’
Second half: you throw a single basket of earth onto level ground. Legge — ‘the advancing with it is my own going forward.’
The symmetry is the argument. Quitting and continuing are equally yours; neither is something that happens to you.
Legge attaches it to learning, which is how the passage is traditionally read: study is a mound you build one basket at a time and can abandon at any height.
Nothing in either half concerns pace. Slowness is simply not the subject.
context.pull: Confucius does not say slow is fine. He says that if you stopped, you stopped.
